title: Feasibility of manufacturing high-aspect-ratio hollow tubes of SS410 through wire-arc directed energy deposition
abstract: Abstract This study reports new observations from the fabrication of high-aspect-ratio hollow tubes of SS410 through wire-arc directed energy deposition (wire-arc DED) process. Characterisation work was performed on a single tube as a function of its build height. The maximum ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1372 MPa and maximum yield strength (YS) of 980 MPa were achieved in the middle region of the tube. The highest UTS in the middle was attributed to the low delta ferrite content. The reduction of delta ferrite was found to be linked with the repetitive heating and cooling. In contrast, the top and bottom sections exhibit a substantial presence of delta ferrite, indicating that the cyclic effects were not considerable. Nevertheless, the presence of significant ductility in the bottom region of the component indicated the occurrence of tempering effects. This observation is further supported by the lower levels of local strain observed using KAM mapping. Overall, this work proposes a novel fabrication method for producing hollow sections with superior strength and ductile properties.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The conventional method of producing hollow tubes for defense application involves a sequential process comprising of rod cutting, drilling, reaming, rifling and lapping. This traditional methodology involves extensive energy and scrapping of material. A sustainable strategy is desirable to produce these components. AM offers immense prospects in this area, and not only it can benefit civil applications but also the defense applications [ 1 ]. To fully realise these benefits, the rapidity in the manufacturing process with AM machines is essential, and this can only be achieved with a high deposition rate [ 2 ]. Across a host of AM processes, wire-arc DED can be considered a rapid AM process thanks to its deposition efficiency ranging from 3 to 7 kg/h [ 3 ]. The wire-arc DED process incorporates wire feeding and an electrical arc as the principal heating means to deposit layers in an orderly manner. Contrary to the LPBF process that uses powder as a feedstock, the expenses of procuring metallic wire are significantly less, reducing overall production expenditure [ 4 ]. Another distinction pertains to the notably high HI characteristic of the wire-arc DED process.

The wire-arc DED process typically utilises HI ranging from 10 to 100 s of J/mm [ 5 ]. This significant parameter exerts an impact on both the microscopic structure as well as the geometric characteristics of the component. The heat buildup within the part rises as the formation height progresses during the layer-by-layer deposition process [ 6 ]. Hence, to create substantial components, minimising the heat generated during the manufacturing method is imperative. Thus, the issue related to the elevated HI can be addressed through two methods: firstly, by considering the type of metal transfer method employed during the procedure [ 7 ], and secondly by selecting feasible process parameters that incorporate reduced HI [ 8 ]. In the present article, the work was directed on both criteria to obtain low-energy input during processing. Therefore, the CMT methodology has been identified as a practical approach for mitigating the adverse effects associated with heat [ 5 ]. The process of CMT integrates an innovative wire feed apparatus alongside advanced digital control mechanisms to manage material deposition while minimising HI effectively [ 9 ].

The CMT-based wire-arc DED technology has been successfully employed with wide-ranging feedstocks including SS [ 10 ], aluminum [ 11 ], copper [ 12 ], titanium alloys [ 13 ] and Inconel [ 14 ]. By maintaining the process variables at their optimal levels, the mechanical properties of certain materials are shown to get enhanced or be retained when compared to their traditional counterparts. Xi et al. [ 15 ] and Bhujangrao et al. [ 16 ] found that the Inconel 718 manufactured using the wire-arc DED method have properties equivalent to the wrought Inconel 718. The same observation with the superior properties was discovered for other materials such as the aluminum alloys [ 17 ,  18 ], Ni–Al-Bronze alloy [ 19 ] and steel [ 20 ,  21 ].

The current information available about the martensitic SS (in particular grade SS410) in the AM community is scarce. However, there are some endeavours on powder-based DED processes. Khodabakhshi et al. [ 22 ] fabricated SS410-L material using a powder-based DED process. Compared to the traditional counterpart, their results demonstrated a significant improvement in the YS and UTS of the SS410 component. Han et al. [ 23 ] utilised the novel approach of UAM for fabricating parts using SS410 feedstock. The UAM-manufactured SS410 after hot isostatic pressing rivals the mechanical strength to those of the original bulk material. The adoption of SS410 in the domain of AM has demonstrated its superiority over traditional components in terms of its mechanical properties. However, when it comes to large-scale AM technologies such as wire-arc DED, welding martensitic steels presents challenges owing to their vulnerability to many types of cracking, including hydrogen-driven cracking [ 24 ], cold cracking [ 25 ] and solidification cracking [ 26 ]. Despite the mentioned defects, the literature reports successful production of SS410 using CMT-based wire-arc DED technique [ 27 ]. Recently, SS410 materials produced using CMT-based wire-arc DED showed superior properties than conventional parts. The work of Roy et al. [ 28 ] involving fabrication of SS410 specimens utilising the CMT-based wire-arc DED procedure is also noticeable. The primary goal of this work was to examine the anisotropy in thin wall structures through the evaluation of their mechanical properties. The findings demonstrated a significant level of anisotropy, as evidenced by a standard deviation of 92 MPa in the UTS measurement. The higher anisotropy was mainly attributable to the heterogeneity of the microstructure composed of varying percentages of tempered and untempered martensite and delta ferrite. In their subsequent research, Roy et al. [ 29 ] conducted an investigation related to the influence of different compositions of the protecting gas onto the microstructure and mechanical properties of SS410. The researchers suggested employing a shielding mixture of 98% argon (Ar) and 3% nitrogen (N 2 ) as a suitable mixture to get the UTS of 1350 MPa with reduced anisotropy and lower delta ferrite content. Considering its adverse effect, the study by Zhu et al. [ 30 ] employed suitable process settings to prevent the development of delta ferrite in the microstructure. Consequently, this approach resulted in exceptional UTS values of 1275 and 1371 MPa in the perpendicular and parallel directions of the build respectively. Nevertheless, elevated UTS was accompanied by a reduction in ductility. Hence, considering the cost-effectiveness, superior properties and easy accessibility of feedstock material, the utilisation of SS410 as a feedstock to develop hollow tubes, albeit challenging, carries considerable incentives. The HI values reported in the literature are significantly high which poses obstacle to manufacture high-aspect-ratio hollow tubes as per the prescribed dimensions. Taking into account the geometrical requirements, the characteristics of a single circular layer at various WFS and TS values were firstly explored and optimised which are reported here as the best parameters to obtain an acceptable level of mechanical properties.

There are certain drawbacks associated with the published research papers related to mechanical properties evaluation. The literature proposed instances of heterogeneities in the microstructure along the build height [ 5 ,  31 ,  32 ]. Therefore, the evaluation of the mechanical properties in the localised region becomes evident to understand the effect of inhomogeneity on the strength. However, a vast majority of studies employs a dog-bone shape with a minimum overall length of 100 mm to assess the strength values. Hence, these large-sized specimens exemplify the variety of microstructures found within the specimen and provide the mean strength measurements. To assess the localised strength values, the assessment through miniature samples was carried out. Moreover, when dealing with cylinders of significant diameters, it may suffice to consider them as solid walls. Most of the articles in the literature correspond to the property evaluation of thin and thick walls. However, smaller tubes have not been considered in the literature. Also, it is expected that the small diameter components will exhibit distinct features since heat is localised to a tiny region for the entire time of the weld [ 33 ]. Therefore, this work assessed the feasibility of the formation of a hollow tube using CMT-based wire-arc DED process.

sections.heading: Wire-arc DED processing
paragraphs:
The wire material utilised in the current work for CMT-based wire-arc DED processing was SS410 with a diameter of 1.2 mm. The depositions were made onto mild steel plates measuring 200 mm, 300 mm and 10 mm in length, breadth and thickness, respectively. The alloying compositions of the feedstock and base plate are shown in Table  1 . 
 Table 1 The composition of the base plate and SS410 wire feedstock utilised for processing via the CMT-based wire-arc DED process Composition C Ni Mn Si P S Cu Cr Mo Fe Feedstock wire (410) 0.08 0.27 0.54 0.39 0.02 0.01 0.14 12.5 0.08 bal Base plate (MS) 0.05 - 0.7 0.12 0.016 0.004 - - - bal

Prior to the fabrication process, the substrate was processed with a grinder, followed by a thorough cleaning with ethanol to prevent the contaminants to interfere with the build process. The fabrication process was conducted via a CMT-based welding system (TPS400I, Fronius, Austria), shown in Fig.  1 . The appropriate trajectory of the welding torch was obtained through the utilisation of a 6-axis robot (Kawasaki, 3BA0061N, Japan). The deposition process uses a shielding gas mixture of 98% Ar and 2% oxygen (O 2 ). The decision to use this gaseous mixture was based on a literature study by Zhang et al. [ 34 ]. Fig. 1 The six -axis robot-controlled CMT-based wire-arc DED setup that fabricates 9 mm hollow tubes for defense applications

sections.heading: Selection of parameters
paragraphs: Prior to fabrication, single bead experiments are conducted to ascertain the viable range of operational variables for printing the hollow tubes. The present study was focused on producing a bore with a diameter of 9 mm and a height of 120 mm. Hence, considering the decreased material wastage during post-machining, choosing a minimum bore diameter of 6 mm is preferred. Therefore, single-layer circular beads are deposited using various combinations of process variables, including TS and WFS. Parameters resulting in improper bonding between the initial and final points of the circular bead, or those producing an inner diameter of less than 6 mm, are eliminated. Consequently, the process parameters adopted for hollow tube fabrication are highlighted in green, while those discarded are marked in red, as shown in Fig.  2 (a). Fig. 2 Sequential process of manufacturing involving (a) parameters selection, (b) DED deposition, (c) cutting and (d) turning to obtain the desired shape of the hollow tube

sections.heading: Fabrication of hollow tubes
paragraphs: The variables used for the deposition are specified as ( x ,  y ), where  x  is WFS and  y  is TS. The selected process parameters were (2.5, 60), (2.5, 70), (2.5, 80) and (3, 80). Subsequently, the deposition was conducted onto the mild steel substrate for a build height of 120 mm. Furthermore, the delay time was determined based on the research by Singh et al. [ 35 ], which demonstrated that an 80-s delay between neighbouring layers resulted in enhanced mechanical properties. The adjacent layers were deposited in alternate direction (one clockwise and another anticlockwise) to ensure the proper formation of the standalone parts which is shown in Fig.  2 (b). In line with this, the tubes were extracted from the substrate plate (Fig.  2 (c)) and machined to the desired finish (Fig.  2 (d)).

sections.heading: Mechanical testing
paragraphs: Mechanical testing of the AM part is a crucial step. The geometry of the fabricated components involved constraints related to the tensile sample dimensions as per the ASTM E8. Therefore, miniature tensile testing was opted to get the appropriate strength from the standalone part. The literature provides evidence of the equivalent tensile results of miniature sample compared to the standard samples [ 36 ,  37 – 38 ]. Testing using such samples has inherent advantages related to less material wastage and cost. Varying thermal histories during CMT-based wire-arc DED can also pose challenges, giving rise to a different microstructure along the build height [ 39 ]. Consequently, the tensile testing was carried out at different build heights to assess the localised strength of the tube.

The schematic shown in Fig.  3  represents the step-by-step procedure of preparing the required dog-bone shape and its dimensions. The hollow tube was divided into three sections: bottom, middle and top. A total of 3 samples from each region were tested and reported in terms of average and standard deviation value. The tensile examination was performed utilising the tensile testing equipment (Walter + bai, LFV, Switzerland) at a 0.25 mm/min strain rate. The Vickers microhardness apparatus (Inova Test, Falcon 400, Netherlands) is utilised to evaluate the hardness values associated with various phases. A diamond indenter is employed to apply a force of 0.2 kg-force for 10 s. The ultimate value documented in the research is the mean of ten indentations that correspond to each respective phase. Fig. 3 The visual depiction of the methodology employed for the mechanical properties testing of hollow tubes fabricated using the CMT-based wire-arc DED method

sections.heading: Microstructural characterisation
paragraphs: Following the build process, specimens were extracted from the bottom, middle and top regions of the hollow tube for the purpose of microscopic examination and characterisation. Specimens that were used for this task of field emission SEM (Jeol, Jsm-6610LV, Japan), optical microscope (LEICA, DM2700 M, Germany) and EDS (Oxford Instruments, X-mas, UK) were prepared using emery papers from grade 320 to 2500 followed by diamond polishing. Subsequently, the specimens were immersed in the etchant composed of 10 g CuSo 4 , 40 ml HCl and 40 ml distilled water for 20 s. Additionally, the samples utilised for EBSD (Zeiss, Sigma 500VP, Germany) were obtained by a series of procedures comprising grinding, polishing and electropolishing. The electropolishing procedure entails immersion of all the samples in an electrolyte solution composed of a blend of 20% butoxyethanol with 80% perchloric acid. The EBSD measurements were conducted with a voltage of 15 kV for a duration of 7 s, employing a step size of 120 nm. Moreover, XRD (Malvern Panalytical, Empyrean, UK) instrument was also used for monitoring the phases during the build process. The range of scans was configured to span from 20 to 120°, with an increment size of 0.01°.

sections.heading: Deposition and process variables used
Effect of different process parameters on the production time
paragraphs: The findings discussed above suggest that the build of a single layer takes less duration when using WFS and TS as 2.5, 80 or 3, 80. Despite the reduced duration of the welding process for a single layer, it leads to the longest total production time for the fabrication of the tube having a height of 120 mm. This phenomenon has been elucidated through Fig.  5 a. Fig. 5 ( a)  The correlation in terms of its number of layers, average height per bead and volumetric material flow per unit length and ( b)  the density values estimated using Archimedes principle of different tubes fabricated utilising the CMT-based wire-arc DED process

Figure  5 a illustrates a correlation between the volume flow rate, in line to the study of Yildiz et al. [ 43 ], average height per bead (total height/ number of layers) and total layers. The data demonstrates a negative correlation between average height per bead and volume flow rate with the number of layers. The volume flow rate of 2.5, 80 exhibits the lowest value, resulting in a decrease of the average height per bead. As a result, this causes a rise in the quantity of layers. The augmentation in the quantity of layers required to construct a tube with a height of 120 mm results in the increase of duration to manufacture. On the other hand, the total number of layers in a 2.5, 60 built tubes was significantly less owing to its larger volume flow rate and average height per bead. It is noteworthy that despite the similarity in HI values between the 2.5, 60 and 3, 80 tubes, there exists a notable variance in the average height per bead and, consequently, the overall production time. The primary factor contributing to this phenomenon primarily relates to the elevated electrical current, which consequently leads to the generation of a substantial arc force on the weld pool [ 44 ]. The arc force direction orients in a similar manner that opposes the vertical dimension, leading to a decrease in height and consequently yielding a lower average height per bead for the 3, 80 tube [ 45 ].

sections.heading: Porosity estimations
paragraphs: The calculated porosity varies from 1.3 to 1.6% for different tubes. No trend was observed in the porosity as a function of the process parameters. However, compared to the other reported studies, the porosity values in this work obtained were apparently higher [ 27 ]. Hence, the primary factor contributing to the relatively higher porosity seen in this study was due to the utilisation of a low HI during the production. To ascertain the specific nature of the pores, the optical analysis revealed the absence of any lack of fusion defects, thus confirming the existence of pores that are linked to the trapping of protective gas within the weld pool.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties of hollow tubes
paragraphs: The stress–strain curve associated with each tube is shown in Fig.  6 . These curves possess notable variations in their properties along the build direction, providing evidence of anisotropy within the component. This variance in the properties is quite evident due to the presence of heterogeneity of the microstructure. Figure  7  illustrates the values of UTS, YS, percentage elongation and hardness values along the build height. The measured values of UTS (Fig.  7 a), YS (Fig.  7 b) and percentage elongation (Fig.  7 c) are well above the benchmarked properties required for the fabrication of defense component [ 47 ]. The maximum and minimum UTS of 1372 MPa and 1175 MPa were observed in the 2.5, 60 tubes followed by 1350 MPa and 1202 MPa in 3, 80 tubes. Moreover, according to the international standard, the required YS and percentage elongation values must be greater than 700 MPa and 16%. Fortunately, the minimum value of YS determined in this study was 820 MPa, and the percentage elongation was 16%. The hardness values were superior as compared to standard properties. However, during the hardness measurement at different positions, some values were found to be below the threshold needed for conventional hollow tubes for defense applications, necessitating specific attention (Fig.  7 d). Certain trend was observed in the mechanical properties as a function of build height from bottom to top. For 2.5, 60 and 3, 80, the UTS values first increase from bottom to the middle and then reduce from the middle to the top. A similar type of variation in the UTS for both tubes can be ascribed to the similar HI during the deposition process (Table  2 ). On the other hand, 2.5, 70 and 2.5, 80 represent a rise in the strength along the build direction. This may also be interlinked with the HI; however, the in-depth analysis of this trend is not in the scope of the present research article. Fig. 6 The stress–strain curve for tubes built with different WFS and TS using the CMT-based wire-arc DED method Fig. 7 The mechanical properties like  a  UTS,  b  YS,  c  percentage elongation and  d  hardness (HV) as a function of build height (bottom, middle and top) associated with hollow tubes fabricated using the CMT-based wire-arc DED

sections.heading: Selection of superior hollow tube for further analysis
paragraphs: A comprehensive analysis was conducted on the best optimal parameter chosen for the fabrication of the hollow tube. It is worthwhile to note that the properties reported through this work are superior for all possible parameters (compared to standard properties for defense application) and this provides the flexibility among the manufacturer to select any of these during fabrication. Therefore, the selection was made on the basis of the highest UTS value and lowest production time. Based on the specified criteria, the tube with 2.5, 60 was determined to be appropriate and chosen for comprehensive analysis.

The variation in the mechanical properties in 2.5, 60 was investigated with respect to the build height from bottom to top. The average UTS and YS exhibit an upward trend as one moves from the bottom to the middle, with values increasing from 1175 to 1372 MPa for UTS and from 910 to 980 MPa for YS. However, as one progresses towards the top, both UTS and YS experience a decline, reaching values of 1202 MPa and 805 MPa, respectively. Conversely, the percentage elongation exhibits a decline from the bottom (25.5%) to the middle part (18%), followed by an upsurge in the top sample (22.5%). To ascertain the underlying factors behind these specific trends in mechanical properties, a microstructural analysis was conducted using a range of materials characterisation methods discussed next.

sections.heading: Phase identification using OM and XRD
paragraphs: Figure  8  shows the optical images of the hollow tube (2.5, 60) at various regions marked as B (bottom), M (middle) and T (top). The microstructure consists of dual phases with different contrasts, i.e. dark and bright. The presence of matrix phase (martensite) is indicated by the dark form evident from the microstructure. Additionally, the second phase, which manifests as a bright, can exist as either RA or delta ferrite. However, to confirm the same, XRD analysis was conducted, as shown in Fig.  9 . Based on the XRD, there was no discernible diffraction pattern observed that corresponds to the presence of RA. The XRD data obtained indicates that the predominant phases present in bottom, middle and top microstructures were BCC delta ferrite and martensite. Moreover, it is essential to emphasise the difficulty of differentiating the BCC and BCT structures of martensite. Therefore, to confirm the crystal structure of martensite, the c/a ratio was evaluated, as shown in Table  3 . The data revealed that the c/a ratio of all three samples exhibits a consistent value of unity throughout various build heights. This finding provides evidence for the existence of martensite as BCC in the microstructure. The existence of such a phase is ascribed to the low carbon percentage in the wire composition. Moreover, the presence of delta ferrite was further confirmed by the ferrite factor calculated using various empirical formulas like Newhouse, Kalenhauser, Schneider and Schaffler [ 48 ]. The ferrite factor can be defined as the difference between chromium ( Cr eq ) and nickel equivalent ( Ni eq ), evaluated for the wire composition used in the present investigation. According to the investigation of Sam et al. [ 48 ] and Zala et al. [ 49 ], it has been interpreted that when the ferrite factor exceeds a value of 10, there exists a potential for the development of delta ferrite in the molten pool. The tabulated numbers shown in Table  4  demonstrate values corresponding to each formula larger than 10. This further validates the occurrence of delta ferrite in the produced component. The delta ferrite was quantified using ImageJ analysis conducted on ten different microscopy images of each sample. The findings indicated a decrease in delta ferrite content from the bottom to the middle, followed by an increase from the middle to the top. The literature confirms the existence of delta ferrite with island-like morphology in martensitic stainless steel [ 27 ,  28 ]. sections.heading: SEM and EDS analysis
paragraphs: SEM study was conducted to identify the specific substructures found in both martensite and delta ferrite (Fig.  10 ). According to the EDS shown in Fig.  11 , the existence silicon oxide precipitations were discovered in the substructures of delta ferrite on the bottom and top samples. However, no such precipitates were identified in the middle specimen. Moreover, the martensitic structure was characterised by the presence of packets containing distinct blocks (Fig.  10 a, b, c) that are oriented in several orientations across all samples. In addition to the presence of block martensite, tempered martensite was detected in the bottom samples (Fig.  10 a). Fig. 10 The low and high magnification microstructures of SS410 samples at various build heights, designated as  a  bottom,  b  middle and  c  top, developed using the CMT-based wire-arc DED technique Fig. 11 The areal composition mapping using EDS at the delta ferrite region of  a  bottom and  b  top sample fabricated by CMT-based wire-arc DED technique

The EDS analysis was carried out to understand the effect of CMT-based wire-arc DED processing on different composition elements as a function of build height. The compositional mapping of the delta ferrite has been shown in Fig.  11 . The mapping was done in the specific region designated as EDS-1 in Fig.  10 (a1) of the bottom sample and EDS-2 in Fig.  10 (c1) of the top sample. According to the results, it was observed that the precipitation of silicon oxide took place. However, no such precipitate was observed in the middle sample. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the hardness of the delta ferrite in the topmost section was slightly higher in comparison to the specimens at the bottom and middle regions. Besides, the reduced martensitic hardness was observed in the bottom part (Fig.  12 ). Fig. 12 Vickers microhardness measurement of delta ferrite and martensite phases observed at the bottom, middle and top portion

The SEM image of fractured surfaces is shown in Fig.  13 . It can be interpreted that the percentage area reduction after fracture was highest at the bottom (Fig.  13 a) and least at the middle (Fig.  13 b) specimen. The significant decrease in percentage area of the samples indicated a high level of ductility. The low magnification image indicated the occurrence of voids and dimple formation in the bottom sample. Apart from the mentioned features, the middle sample also exhibits cleavages that represent the brittle mode of failure. It justified the low percentage area reduction in the middle region. Moreover, the top sample (Fig.  13 c) shows the dimples with certain region of cleavage facets. Moreover, the void formation refers to the low HI incorporated in the current investigation to form the desired standalone component. Fig. 13 The tensile fracture surfaces obtained at different build height marked as  a  bottom,  b  middle and  c  top in low and high magnifications (D: Dimples, V: Voids and C: Cleavage)

sections.heading: EBSD analysis
paragraphs: The IPF and PF maps are shown in Fig.  14 , and they present the occurrence of martensitic lath as well as the contents of delta ferrite. The orientation of delta ferrite was almost the same in each case within the samples at specified build height. However, the orientation of delta ferrite in top samples (Fig.  14 c) differs from the bottom (Fig.  14 a) and middle Fig.  14 b. Fig. 14 The IPF and PF obtained using EBSD of CMT-based wire-arc DED fabricated samples at various build height designated as bottom, middle and top

The PF for the (100), (110) and (111) planes are also shown in Fig.  14 . The PF clearly indicated that the grain boundaries in the bottom sample are oriented in a preferred direction; however, it is important to note that even after preferred orientation, the extent of anisotropy (as seen in standard deviation value of Fig.  7 ) was high due to the large amount of delta ferrite in the bottom section which seems to be in accord with the observation made by Roy et al. [ 28 ]. On the other hand, the middle sample with preferred orientation and fewer content of delta ferrite presented less anisotropy in the UTS values. The top samples exhibit random distribution of the grain orientation and a higher extent of anisotropy.

Moreover, GOS can be defined as the mean misorientation of a particular grain. It is determined by taking the mean of misorientation of each pixel (decided by step size) within a single grain. The GOS parameter proves to be highly advantageous in discerning various kinds of structures that exist inside the microstructure. Khajuria et al. [ 50 ] and Wang et al. [ 51 ] utilised the same approach to differentiate various microstructures. The value of GOS usually varies from 0 to 7.4°. The grain is classified as recrystallised (blue), partially recrystallised (yellow), or deformed (red) based on the value of GOS [ 50 ]. As shown in Fig.  15 b, the specimen positioned in the middle exhibit a 29.4% distorted microstructure. In contrast, the percentage of distortion in the bottom (Fig.  15 a) and top (Fig.  15 c) were just 19.3% and 10.4%, respectively. Furthermore, it was observed that the middle specimen exhibits a recrystallised and partially recrystallised structural proportion of 29.2% and 40.1%, respectively, which is significantly lower in comparison to the middle and top samples. Besides, the extent of recrystallised microstructure within 0–1° of GOS mapping was higher for the bottom samples (Fig.  15 d). Fig. 15 The grain orientation spread (GOS) mapping of samples at various build height fabricated using the CMT-based wire-arc DED technique

The impact of plastic strain on the overall quality of diffraction patterns is widely acknowledged [ 52 ]. Hence, IQ mapping is employed to access the amount of plastic strain in the form of dislocations in the samples. In the IQ map, sections of the microstructure experiencing strain can be visually represented as darker [ 53 ]. The darker region in the IQ mapping was lowest for bottom samples (50%) than for the middle (71%) and top (64%) samples (Fig.  16 a). Furthermore, it is crucial to observe that the delta ferrite grains depicted in the map exhibit no deformation. However, with the rise in the delta ferrite percentage, the amount of strain or dislocations in the sample gets reduced. According to the microscopy analysis, the middle samples contain the least delta ferrite; hence, the strain associated with it would be comparatively higher than the top and bottom samples. Fig. 16 a  IQ,  b  KAM and  c  GND mapping obtained using EBSD as a function of build height

Moreover, KAM map was used to evaluate the local strain in different grains at the bottom, middle and top portion of the samples (Fig.  16 b). KAM measurement estimated the degree of distortion inside a grain [ 54 ,  55 ]. It has been observed that high strain is associated with martensite. The single grain of delta ferrite showed no deformities. Also, the extent of strain was significantly reduced in the bottom samples. On the other hand, bottom and middle samples reflect high local strains within the martensitic structures [ 56 ]. This high degree of strain can be ascribed to the occurrence of GND in the middle and top specimens (Fig.  16 c). Comparing KAM and GND mapping with GOS, it is essential to emphasise that recrystallised region and delta ferrite exhibit a low degree of strain and are devoid of dislocations. In contrast, deformed or uncrystallised grains possess a substantial strain with abundant of dislocations.

A variety of grains gets formed during CMT-based wire-arc DED processed hollow tube. The variation in the grain size from 1.16 to 38, 0.8 to 25 and 1.39 to 42 µm was observed in the top, middle and bottom samples, respectively. As depicted in Fig.  17 , the maximum grain size is linked with the island-type delta ferrite. The delta ferrite size was lower in the middle samples when compared with the top and bottom samples. Moreover, it is expected that an increase in the variability of grain size could result from an increased anisotropy, as seen by the standard deviation in the value of UTS. Fig. 17 Grain size mapping of (a) bottom, (b) middle and (c) top specimens fabricated by CMT-based wire-arc DED technique

sections.heading: Discussions
paragraphs: This feasibility study was aimed at assessing the viability to manufacture a 9-mm hollow tube through the CMT-based wire-arc DED process. The evaluation primarily focuses on the mechanical properties of the desired component. The values of UTS, YS and percentage elongation found in this study surpass the specifications that are necessary to fabricate the tubes for defense applications (Fig.  7 a, b, c). On the contrary, the hardness corresponding to the delta ferrite phase exhibits a lower degree of acceptable quality when compared to established attributes, necessitating specific consideration. As depicted in Fig.  12 , the findings indicated a considerable variation in the values from 180 HV (delta ferrite) to 338 HV (martensite). In order to achieve specified hardness, the microstructure must be free of the delta ferrite phase. The presence of delta ferrite in the microstructure is detrimental to hardness and toughness properties [ 57 ].

The existence of blocky-type delta ferrite is confirmed by various studies in the literature [ 58 ]. The reason for delta ferrite formation lies in the wire composition containing less Ni content. Ni, an austenite stabiliser, increases the phase field of austenite, reducing the possibility of ferrite in the steel [ 59 ]. However, less Ni amount stabilises the delta content even further and results in its retention at room temperature. Also, the occurrence of the same is confirmed using ferrite factor evaluation (Table  4 ) and XRD analysis (Fig.  9 ).

The quantification analysis (Fig.  8 ) showed the delta ferrite to be 35% less in the middle region than the top and bottom. This difference can be attributed to cyclic thermal treatment that took place in the middle sample due to the repetitive cooling and heating of the sample [ 60 ]. This effect is evident due to the continuous formation of different layers over the middle section. It is noteworthy that, despite the significant number of thermal cycles experienced by the bottom sample, there are no observed changes in the delta ferrite content. This observation indicates that an increase in thermal cycles alone does not solely influence delta ferrite dissolution. Instead, the peak temperature plays a crucial role in the elimination of delta ferrite. For effective dissolution, the peak temperature must reside within the austenitic regime [ 61 ]. If this condition is not met, delta ferrite will not be eliminated from the parent phase despite thermal cycling. Contrary to bottom region, the delta ferrite dissolution in the middle is the result of higher number of cycles with peak temperature in austenitic regime. Also, the thinning of the precipitates at the grain boundary was observed in the SEM image as shown in Fig.  10 . After the complete elimination of precipitates, the subsequent cycle resulted in the size reduction of delta ferrite (Fig.  8 ), and therefore, improved mechanical properties were obtained in the middle portion of 2.5, 60 tube (Fig.  7 ) [ 61 ].

The other more pronounced effect of cyclic heat treatment is the formation of distorted microstructure in the martensite of the middle section. The GOS map (Fig.  15 ) provides evidence of the same, which showed the highest deformed region (shown in red). Its reason can be ascribed to the occurrence of two types of phases in the microstructure. The coefficient of thermal expansion of martensite [ 62 ] is lower as compared to the delta ferrite [ 63 ], so during the continuous heating and cooling, the phases undergo repetitive expansion and contraction (Fig.  18 ). During the heating process, it emerges that the delta ferrite phase exhibits a greater expansion in comparison to the matrix phase. Consequently, this expansion leads to the development of tensile residual stress inside the martensite phase. However, during the cooling, the reverse happens, resulting in the compressive residual stress in martensite. As a result of this impact in the middle section, the overall outcome is the formation of compressive residual stresses in the phase with a small coefficient of thermal expansion, i.e. martensite, and consequently, the distorted martensitic structure is formed as confirmed by the GOS mapping. Furthermore, it is crucial to acknowledge that the GOS mapping has demonstrated a correlation with the locked-up stress experienced in the microstructure. Field et al. [ 64 ] were the first to employ GOS for assessing residual stress at the scale of certain microns. The presence of elevated GOS levels in the middle region of the tube indicated a significant amount of stored energy inside the grains, resulting from the residual stress induced by repeated cycles of heating and cooling [ 65 ]. In support of the stated justification, Huang et al. [ 66 ] have previously reported a comparable investigation, confirming the existence of compressive residual stress in the middle section of a hollow tube. Additionally, the reduction in the delta ferrite percentage, contributed to the contraction throughout the cooling process, was verified by the measurement of delta ferrite using optical microscopy. As compared to the bottom and top samples, this distortion in the middle has also led to the reduction of percentage elongation to 18.7%. In addition, along with the reduction of delta ferrite, the occurrence of compressive residual stresses in the middle section also leads to enhanced mechanical properties [ 67 ], which showed 16.7% and 14.4% improvement in the UTS and 7.7% and 21.7% improvement in the YS values as compared to bottom and top samples, respectively. Fig. 18 Schematic representation of dual phase system with different coefficients of thermal expansion during repetitive heating and cooling

Moreover, it is vital to point out that the consequence of cyclic heat treatment was not pronounced in the bottom section because as the build height increases, the peak temperature associated with the bottom region decreases [ 68 ]. As studied by Singh et al. [ 60 ], the effect of cyclic thermal treatment becomes more evident when the temperature is high (above 950 °C) as expected in the middle portion. However, it is anticipated that such temperature was not achieved in the bottom samples for most of the thermal cycles; hence, cyclic heat treatment is insignificant in the bottom region. For most cycles, the temperature might be in the tempering range, resulting in the tempered martensite (Fig.  10 a), whose effect can be seen in the mechanical properties having low strength and high ductility due to dimple formations (Figs.  7 ,  13 a) and low martensitic hardness (Fig.  12 ) of bottom samples. Furthermore, the qualitative analysis shows low deformations by IQ mapping (Fig.  16 a), low strain values (Fig.  16 b) and reduced overall GND values (Fig.  16 c) and, hence, provides additional evidence supporting the presence of tempering in the bottom sample.

As per the literature, if the delta ferrite present in CMT-based wire-arc DED fabricated samples has a similar orientation then it indicates that it has formed during the solidification process rather than during thermal cycling [ 28 ]. However, the orientation of delta ferrite in the middle and bottom samples is the same as (101). According to the GOS maps, it has fully recrystallised. This shows that the delta ferrite in the bottom and middle region results from recrystallisation due to thermal cycling. Conversely, the delta ferrite grain in the top sample exhibits a partial recrystallised state with some number of dislocations (shown as green colour in delta ferrite of top samples), confirmed using GND mapping in Fig.  16  and resulting in the highest hardness of 205 HV. Besides, the low hardness in the same phase of the bottom (180 HV) and middle (187 HV) is attributed to the 101 (Fig.  14 ) plane that manifests the highest level of mobility as a slip plane in BCC crystal formations [ 69 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This novel work investigated the feasibility to manufacture a 9-mm hollow tube through a single shot process using CMT-based wire-arc DED method. The assessment focuses on the mechanical attributes of the fabricated component. The preliminary analysis revealed four suitable parameters for controlling the quality of manufacturing. Based on the evidence presented, the following broad conclusions can be made: The strength and ductility values associated with each tube exceeded the specified values for their proposed usage in defense applications. The hardness values in some of the regions were found to be inappropriate and hence provide the further processing for their improvement. Among the four tubes produced, WFS and TS values of 2.5 and 60 respectively led to the manufacture of improved mechanical properties and shorter production duration. The reduced production time can be attributed to the high-volume flow rate associated with the parameters during the part fabrication. The UTS, YS and percentage elongation exhibit notable degrees of anisotropy along the build height, likely attributable to the presence of an inhomogeneous microstructure. Comparing the bottom, middle and top region of the 2.5, 60 hollow tube, it was observed that the UTS value increases by 16.7% from bottom to middle and then reduces by 14% from middle to top. Middle region exhibited low delta ferrite content of 12%. This is owing to the strong impact of cyclic heat treatment on the middle region. The relatively greater fraction of deformed structure (29.4%) was present in the middle region which is due to the obvious reasons of cyclic heat treatment. Conversely, the bottom and top regions show comparatively less content of the same. The occurrence of tempered martensite in the bottom region resulted in the high percentage elongation (25.5%) when compared with the top and middle regions. The study suggests the effective production of hollow tubes exhibiting higher strength and ductility characteristics. Based on the findings pertaining to various qualities, it is crucial to acknowledge the concerns associated with the degree of anisotropy and the relatively low hardness values at some regions. Post-processing can be a viable option to consider as a feasible alternative prior to the practical use of the manufactured component.
